**Predicted Finish and Marks (Shanghai Diamond League, 16 May 2026)**  

1. **Armand Duplantis (SWE)** – 6.12 m  
2. **Emmanouil Karalis (GRE)** – 6.01 m  
3. **Sondre Guttormsen (NOR)** – 5.95 m  
4. **Kurtis Marschall (AUS)** – 5.92 m  
5. **Sam Kendricks (USA)** – 5.88 m  
6. **Zachery Bradford (USA)** – 5.85 m  
7. **Thibaut Collet (FRA)** – 5.82 m  
8. **Menno Vloon (NED)** – 5.78 m  
9. **Bokai Huang (CHN)** – 5.70 m  
10. **Chenyang Li (CHN)** – 5.55 m  

---

**Reasoning**

The Shanghai Diamond League meet on 16 May 2026 falls early in the outdoor season, so athletes’ indoor form and their ability to transition quickly to outdoor conditions are key. Recent performance data from late 2025 and early 2026 provide strong indicators.

**1. Armand Duplantis** – The clear favourite. His indoor campaign was historic: a world record of 6.31 m in Uppsala (March 2026) and a comfortable 6.25 m to win the World Indoor title in Toruń. Outdoors, he has consistently opened near 6.10 m in previous years (e.g., 6.10 in Berlin and 6.11 in Shaoxing in 2025). Given his unmatched consistency and ability to rise to competition, a winning mark of 6.12 m is a conservative estimate. He will likely clear 6.00 m on his first attempt and then push toward a meet record.

**2. Emmanouil Karalis** – The Greek athlete has firmly established himself as the world’s second-best vaulter. His indoor season included a Greek record of 6.17 m (February 2026) and a silver medal at the World Indoor Championships (6.05 m). He has a strong head‑to‑head record against everyone except Duplantis, regularly finishing second behind him in Diamond League events (e.g., Xiamen, Shaoxing, Oslo, Monaco in 2025). He also cleared 6.00 m or better in multiple outdoor meets last year. Expect him to be the only one challenging Duplantis, likely finishing at 6.01 m.

**3. Sondre Guttormsen** – The Norwegian has made a significant leap in the past year. His indoor 2026 featured a stunning 6.06 m in Rouen and 6.00 m at the Mondo Classic, followed by a 5.95 m for 4th at the World Indoor Championships. Outdoors in 2025 he reached 5.90 m at the World Championships (6th) and showed he can handle big stages. His upward trajectory and recent ability to consistently clear 5.90+ m put him ahead of the rest of the pack. A 5.95 m outdoor opener is realistic, especially with the confidence from his indoor exploits.

**4. Kurtis Marschall** – The Australian bronze medalist from the 2025 World Championships (5.95 m) has proven he can compete at the top level. His indoor 2026 was very strong: a 6.00 m win in Clermont-Ferrand and a 6.00 m bronze at the World Indoor Championships. However, he recorded a no‑height at the Australian Championships in April 2026, which raises a slight concern about his outdoor rhythm. Still, his consistent 5.90–6.00 m range and prior Diamond League podiums (e.g., 3rd in Monaco, 3rd in Chorzów in 2025) suggest he will bounce back with a solid 5.92 m here.

**5. Sam Kendricks** – At 33, the American three-time world champion is still a formidable competitor, but his peak heights have declined slightly. He managed 5.95 m for 4th at the 2025 World Championships, and his indoor 2026 best is 5.90 m (Uppsala). His outdoor results in 2025 were mostly in the 5.80–5.85 m range (e.g., 5.82 m in Monaco, 5.80 m in Silesia). He has the experience to perform well under pressure, but he no longer has the margin to challenge the top three. A 5.88 m is a fair prediction.

**6. Zachery Bradford** – The American indoor champion (6.01 m at US Indoor Championships in February 2026) has shown he can clear 5.90 m indoors repeatedly (five times in 2026). Outdoors, he won the Drake Relays Vault at Jordan Creek with 5.83 m in April. However, he had a no‑height in the main Drake Relays competition. His outdoor consistency is still developing; he is likely to be competitive for 5.85 m but may struggle if the bar goes higher than 5.90 m.

**7. Thibaut Collet** – The French record holder (5.95 m outdoor, 5.92 m indoor) had a solid 2025 outdoor season, finishing 5th at the World Championships (5.90 m) and 2nd at the Athletissima Lausanne Diamond League (5.82 m). However, his 2026 indoor form was less impressive: a best of 5.85 m and only 8th at the World Indoor Championships. He tends to be slightly more consistent in Europe than in Asia. A 5.82 m is a reasonable ceiling here.

**8. Menno Vloon** – The Dutch vaulter was European indoor champion in 2025 but has struggled to replicate that outdoors. His 2026 indoor best is 5.85 m, and he has not cleared 5.90 m outdoors since mid‑2025 (e.g., 5.90 m in Chorzów, 5.92 m in Berlin). His recent results (7th at World Indoor, 8th in Uppsala) suggest he is slightly off his best. A 5.78 m is a realistic prediction.

**9. Bokai Huang** – The Chinese veteran has a personal best of 5.80 m outdoors and 5.75 m indoors. His 2025 season included a 5.85 m win in Madrid, but he was inconsistent—no‑heights in Düsseldorf and at the World Championships qualification. His 2026 outdoor start has been poor: a no‑height at the National Athletics Grand Prix in early May. He may struggle to surpass 5.70 m in front of a home crowd.

**10. Chenyang Li** – The young Chinese record holder (5.86 m indoors in March 2026) had a promising indoor season but has faltered outdoors. His last outdoor result (9 May 2026) was a mere 5.30 m, indicating either injury or a major form dip. He lacks the experience to handle a high‑level Diamond League field at this stage, so a 5.55 m finish is plausible.

### Predicted Finish – Women's Shot Put, Shanghai Diamond League, 16 May 2026

1. **Chase Jackson (USA)** – **20.52 m**  
2. **Jessica Schilder (NED)** – **20.18 m**  
3. **Sarah Mitton (CAN)** – **19.92 m**  
4. **Yemisi Mabry (GER)** – **19.85 m**  
5. **Jaida Ross (USA)** – **19.38 m**  
6. **Danniel Thomas-Dodd (JAM)** – **19.25 m**  
7. **Fanny Roos (SWE)** – **19.10 m**  
8. **Linru Zhang (CHN)** – **19.05 m**  
9. **Jiayuan Song (CHN)** – **18.92 m**  
10. **Maggie Ewen (USA)** – **18.75 m**

---

### Analysis & Reasoning

**1. Chase Jackson (20.52 m)**  
Jackson is the clear favourite. The reigning two-time world outdoor champion (2022, 2023) and current World Indoor champion (2026, with 20.14 m), she has dominated the event since 2022. Her 2025 outdoor campaign featured a 20.95 m win at the Iron Wood Classic, a 20.94 m at Prefontaine, and a 20.90 m in Brussels. She opened 2026 with a 20.13 m victory in Oklahoma (11 Apr) and a 20.44 m indoor U.S. title. Jackson’s consistency and ability to produce 20.50+ even in early-season meets—she threw 20.31 m in Xiamen last April—make her the overwhelming pick. Expect her to control the competition from the first round.

**2. Jessica Schilder (20.18 m)**  
Schilder, the 2025 world outdoor champion and European indoor champion, has the second-best pedigree in the field. Her 2025 outdoor best of 20.47 m (Dutch record) came in Xiamen, and she won the 2025 Diamond League final in Zürich with 20.26 m. Indoors this winter she threw 20.69 m in Berlin (a Dutch indoor record) and 20.49 m in Apeldoorn. While she placed only 4th at the 2026 World Indoor Championships (19.63 m), that was a slight blip; her overall trajectory is upward. She has yet to contest an outdoor meet in 2026, but her indoor sharpness and technical command suggest a quick adaptation to the outdoor ring. A 20.18 m puts her comfortably ahead of the chasing pack.

**3. Sarah Mitton (19.92 m)**  
Mitton is the 2025 World Indoor champion and 2023 world outdoor silver medallist. Her 2025 outdoor highlights include 20.39 m at Prefontaine and 20.35 m in Guelph. However, her 2026 outdoor debut on 3 May in Albufeira was only 19.02 m—a significant drop from her usual standard. That performance, coupled with a 19.78 m at the 2026 World Indoors (2nd behind Jackson), suggests she is still rounding into peak form. Mitton has the strength and experience to bounce back, and Shanghai’s familiar Diamond League stage should bring out a better throw. A 19.92 m is realistic given her 2025 average in high-level meets, but she will need to find another gear to challenge Schilder.

**4. Yemisi Mabry (19.85 m)**  
The reigning Olympic gold medallist (2024, 20.00 m) has shown excellent indoor form in 2026, winning the German Indoor title with 20.37 m and posting 19.86 m in Nordhausen. She was 5th at the 2026 World Indoors (19.46 m), a slight disappointment after her 2024 Olympic triumph. Outdoors, her 2025 best was 19.78 m (indoor equivalent) but she threw 19.77 m in Nordhausen in 2025 and was a consistent 19.5+ in Diamond League meetings. Mabry’s technique is reliable, but she has yet to break 20 m outdoors consistently. She will battle Mitton for third, but the Canadian’s slightly higher ceiling and proven Diamond League success give Mitton the edge.

**5. Jaida Ross (19.38 m)**  
Ross, 24, is the rising star. The 2024 NCAA champion and fourth-place Olympian, she broke 20 m indoors in 2024 (20.01 m) and threw 20.13 m outdoors at the 2025 Prefontaine Classic (3rd). Her 2026 outdoor season started well with a 19.07 m win at the Oregon Twilight on 8 May. She has been improving steadily, and the Shanghai atmosphere should see her push toward 19.40 m. Her youth and momentum place her ahead of the veteran group below.

**6. Danniel Thomas-Dodd (19.25 m)**  
The 33-year-old Jamaican veteran has been remarkably consistent, with recent outdoor marks of 19.34 m (Athens, 11 Apr 2026) and 19.12 m (Miramar, 4 Apr 2026). She is a former World Indoor silver medallist and Commonwealth champion. While she rarely reaches 19.50 m anymore, she is a reliable 19.2-19.3 performer. Her experience and steady start to 2026 give her an edge over Roos and the Chinese athletes.

**7. Fanny Roos (19.10 m)**  
Roos set the Swedish outdoor record of 19.66 m at this very meeting in 2025 (then called Shanghai). She had a strong 2025 overall, with several 19.4-19.6 m throws. However, her 2026 form has been subdued: she managed only 18.96 m at the World Indoors (6th) and has not yet competed outdoors. At 30, she remains capable of a 19.1-19.2 m throw, but she will need a perfect series to crack the top six.

**8. Linru Zhang (19.05 m)**  
Zhang is China’s second-best hope. She improved significantly in 2025, throwing 19.47 m at the Chinese National Games (November) and 19.29 m in Neubrandenburg. Her 2026 outdoor season has not yet started, but she is coming off a strong indoor campaign (18.89 m in March) and will be motivated by the home crowd. She may be slightly behind Roos but has the upside to threaten for seventh.

**9. Jiayuan Song (18.92 m)**  
Song, the 2024 Olympic bronze medallist, has struggled to replicate that form. Her 2025 best was only 18.95 m (at the Chinese Games), and she opened 2026 with 18.89 m in March. At 28, she is in her prime but appears to have plateaued. The Shanghai crowd will support her, but she lacks the recent 19+ consistency of the athletes above.

**10. Maggie Ewen (18.75 m)**  
Once a top U.S. thrower (4th at 2019 Worlds), Ewen has fallen off sharply. She placed 13th at the 2025 World Championships (17.31 m) and failed to finish her 2026 outdoor meets (DNS and NM in April). Her 2025 best of 19.94 m is a distant memory. Unless she finds a spark, she will be out of contention early.
blurbs.400m Women:
**Predicted Finish & Marks – Women's 400 Metres – Shanghai Diamond League – 16 May 2026**

1. **Salwa Eid Naser (BRN)** – 48.87  
2. **Nickisha Pryce (JAM)** – 49.15  
3. **Aaliyah Butler (USA)** – 49.31  
4. **Roxana Gómez (CUB)** – 49.55  
5. **Stacey Ann Williams (JAM)** – 49.93  
6. **Sada Williams (BAR)** – 50.22  
7. **Martina Weil (CHI)** – 50.41  
8. **Mercy Adongo Oketch (KEN)** – 50.64  
9. **Paris Peoples (USA)** – 50.88  

---

**Preview & Reasoning**

**1. Salwa Eid Naser (BRN) – 48.87**  
Naser remains the class of the field. At 27, she is in her prime and her 2025 World Championships bronze (48.19) was her fastest clocking since 2019. That 48.19 in Tokyo was a full second faster than anyone else in this field has ever run. Her 2026 form is already sharp: she opened with a 48.94 in Bayaguana in March, then went 48.67 in Kingston and 49.33 in Miami during Grand Slam Track. She also ran a slick 22.45 over 200 metres, showing the raw speed to close hard. The only concern is the DQ in Philadelphia and inconsistent Euros-season results (51.08 in Lausanne), but when Naser is focused and healthy, she has a gear nobody here can match. She will control the race from the front and win by a comfortable margin.

**2. Nickisha Pryce (JAM) – 49.15**  
Pryce has blossomed into a consistent sub-49.50 performer. She won the Jamaican title in a lifetime best 49.97 in 2025 and improved to 49.63 in Monaco. At the World Championships, she ran 49.46 in the semi-final and 49.97 in the final – not a medal, but rock-solid. Her 2026 indoor season was mixed (51.29, 52.43), but she ran 22.94 in early May, her 200-metre speed building towards the outdoor season. She is the most reliable Jamaican in this field and has a clear edge over Butler on championship experience. She will push Naser early but lacks the raw power to hold on.

**3. Aaliyah Butler (USA) – 49.31**  
Butler is the young American on the rise. She won the NCAA indoor title in a stunning 49.97, then went 49.26 outdoors to win the NCAA final – that was the second-fastest time in the field behind only Naser’s 48.19. She ran 49.09 in Monaco and 49.86 at the Pre Classic. However, she struggled at the World Championships (50.63 semi-final) and her 2026 start has been more moderate: 50.10 at Tom Jones Memorial and 22.84 in the 200 metres. The talent is undeniable, but she is still learning to execute against elite pros over the full lap. She will be in the mix for a podium spot but may fade slightly if the pace is brutal.

**4. Roxana Gómez (CUB) – 49.55**  
Gómez had a career year in 2025, running 49.48 in the World final and 49.78 in the semis. She also won consistently on the European circuit (50.40, 50.37). Her 2026 has been quiet but solid: 50.74 in March and 50.83 in Bogotá. She is a tough, experienced racer who rarely runs badly, but she lacks the top-end speed of the three ahead of her. She will run a smart, even race and hold off the Jamaican quartet behind her, but she cannot challenge for a top-three finish.

**5. Stacey Ann Williams (JAM) – 49.93**  
Williams is a fascinating case. She ran 49.59 in the World Championship heats (second only to Naser among the field) and 50.08 in the Jamaican final. But her 2026 has been spent running 800 metres (2:02.98) and 300 metres indoors (35.92). That suggests she is experimenting with longer distances. Her raw 400-metre speed may be slightly dulled by the endurance focus. She could dip below 50 seconds, but she likely lacks the specific race sharpness to go much faster.  

**6. Sada Williams (BAR) – 50.22**  
The Barbadian champion has been a consistent 50-low performer for years, but her peak (49.75 in 2022) is now four years behind her. In 2025, she ran 50.39 in the World semi-finals and 50.65 in Chorzów, but her European circuit results were mostly 50.9 or slower. Her 2026 season started with a 51.38 in Kingston and a 51.38 again in April. She is not improving and looks a step slower than the Jamaicans and Cubans. She will fight hard but lacks the closing power she once had.  

**7. Martina Weil (CHI) – 50.41**  
Weil is a high-quality continental-level star but has not made the full leap to global contention. She ran 49.72 in Zürich and 49.83 in Paris in 2025, good for 4th and 3rd in those Diamond Leagues, but she was only 6th in the World final (49.48). Her 2026 has been slower: 51.99 in April. She may be building form, but against this depth, she will struggle to stay under 50 seconds.  

**8. Mercy Adongo Oketch (KEN) – 50.64**  
Oketch is a promising Kenyan record holder (50.14 in 2025). She ran 51.25 indoors at the World Indoor Championships in 2026 (bronze) and 50.17 outdoors in Nairobi. However, her results against top non-African opposition have been less impressive: 51.36 in the World semi-finals and 50.54 in Madrid. She is still learning to compete at this level. The Shanghai Diamond League will be a step up in intensity, and she may be exposed by the deeper quality of the Jamaicans and Americans.  

**9. Paris Peoples (USA) – 50.88**  
Peoples is a solid domestic performer – 2nd at USA Indoors (51.65) and 5th at USAs outdoors (51.27). She has run 51.05 this season and 50.79 in Botswana. But she has never broken 50 seconds, and against seven athletes who have all run under 50.5, she is clearly behind. She will run a gritty race but will be fighting to stay in contact rather than competing for a place in the top half.

---

**Race Dynamics**  
Naser will go out hard and try to break the field by 250 metres. Pryce and Butler will follow closest, with Gómez running steady. The Jamaicans (Stacey Ann Williams and Sada Williams) may battle for 5th but neither looks sharp enough to threaten the podium. Look for Naser to hit the bell in ~23.5 and hold a 1-second lead at 350 metres, then cruise home to a commanding victory.

**Predicted Finish – Men’s 110 Metres Hurdles – Shanghai Diamond League – 16 May 2026**

| Place | Athlete (Country) | Predicted Time |

---

### Preview and Analysis

**Rachid Muratake (JPN) – 13.02**  
The 23-year-old Japanese star enters Shanghai on a clear upward trajectory. His **13.05 (-0.2 m/s) victory in Osaka on 10 May** is the fastest legal outdoor time any competitor in this field has run in 2026. That performance came just six days before this race, giving him both sharpness and confidence. Muratake has consistently improved since his 5th‑place finish at the 2025 World Championships (13.18), and his 12.92 wind‑aided mark in Fukui last summer shows he has sub‑13 potential when conditions align. He also has the home‑continent advantage and will be motivated to claim his first Diamond League scalp.

**Cordell Tinch (USA) – 13.04**  
The reigning World Champion (2025 gold in 12.99) is the class of the field historically, but his 2026 outdoor season has been slow to ignite. His only 110 m hurdle races this spring were **13.59 (+0.7) on 4 April** – a pedestrian time that suggests he is still rebuilding racing sharpness after a winter that included long jump experiments and a 6th‑place finish in the long jump at US Indoors. Tinch’s indoor form (7.52 in February) was respectable, but he has not faced elite competition outdoors yet. He is tactically savvy and will close hard, but the rust factor likely keeps him just behind Muratake. A 13.04 would still be a solid season opener for the world champion.

**Jamal Britt (USA) – 13.10**  
Britt has been the most consistent American so far in 2026, running **13.07 (+0.8) at Miramar** and **13.07 (+1.4) at the Aggie Invitational**, both in April. His indoor season also produced a strong 7.46 at US Indoors. However, he lacks a truly elite win in his recent history – his best 2025 mark was 13.08 at Grand Slam Philadelphia, and he DNF’d in the US Championships final. Britt’s reliability puts him solidly in the 13.0–13.1 range, but he rarely finds another gear to challenge the very top. Expect another honest, well‑raced 13.10.

**Enrique Llopis (ESP) – 13.12**  
Llopis was arguably the most impressive hurdler indoors in 2026, winning the World Indoor silver with **7.42** and dominating the European circuit. That speed should translate outdoors, but he has not raced a 110 m hurdles outdoors yet this season – his last outdoor race was the 2025 World Championships (4th, 13.16). Rust may cost him a few hundredths, but his indoor times (7.45 in Liévin, 7.45 in Madrid) indicate he is in phenomenal condition. A 13.12 debut would be a strong statement, though he may need one more meet to reach full sharpness.

**Orlando Bennett (JAM) – 13.18**  
The 2025 World Championships silver medalist (13.08 PB in Tokyo) is a proven big‑race performer, but his 2026 form has been underwhelming. His only outdoor result this year is **13.33 (+0.8) at the Tom Jones Memorial** on 18 April – nearly three‑tenths off his best. He also ran a modest 13.54 in the heats. Bennett often rises to the occasion at major meets, but this is a standard Diamond League and he appears to be building slowly. He should improve on his season’s best but lacks the sharpness to challenge for the podium.

**Jason Joseph (SUI) – 13.21**  
Joseph’s season has been almost exclusively indoors (7.50 Swiss title in March). He has **no outdoor 110 m hurdles races in 2026** so far, and his 2025 outdoor season peaked at 13.07 but included a DNF in the World Championship final after a promising semi. Joseph is a talented technician who can run 13.1 on a good day, but without recent competition rhythm and facing a deep field, he is likely to settle for a mid‑pack finish.

**Junxi Liu (CHN) – 13.35**  
The Chinese record‑holder for 60 m hurdles (7.47 indoors) and World Indoor bronze medalist has struggled in the early outdoor season. His only 2026 outing at 110 m hurdles was **13.51 (–0.2) in Hiroshima** on 29 April, finishing 4th. That is well off his 13.14 PB from the Chinese National Games. Liu may benefit from racing on home soil, but his current form suggests a time in the 13.3–13.4 range.

**Enzo Diessl (AUT) – 13.48**  
The 21‑year‑old Austrian European U23 champion is still developing. His 2026 indoor best of **7.64** is respectable but not world‑class, and he has not raced outdoors yet this year. Diessl ran 13.20 in the 2025 Silesia Memorial, but a repeat of that seems unlikely given the lack of recent competition. He will gain experience but should finish behind the more seasoned athletes.

**Zhuoyi Xu (CHN) – 13.65**  
The “glasses flyer” has had a nightmare start to 2026. At the Chinese National Grand Prix on 9 May, he ran **14.42 (–1.7) in the heats and 14.07 (–1.0) in the final** – both well above his 13.12 PB. This suggests either an injury or a severe loss of form. Even with home support, he is unlikely to be competitive in this elite field.

**Key factors:** Muratake’s recent 13.05 gives him the edge over the still‑rusty Tinch. Britt and Llopis are both sharp from indoor campaigns but lack the same outdoor velocity. Bennett and Joseph are sleepers who could spring up if they find form, but their limited 2026 outings hold them back. The Chinese pair are clearly off the pace this year. Expect a fast, tactical race with the top four separated by just one‑tenth of a second.
blurbs.Long Jump Women:
**Predicted Finish & Marks (Women's Long Jump – Shanghai Diamond League, 16 May 2026)**  

1. **Alexis Brown (USA)** – **6.97 m**  
2. **Natalia Linares (COL)** – **6.91 m**  
3. **Monae' Nichols (USA)** – **6.87 m**  
4. **Larissa Iapichino (ITA)** – **6.83 m**

9. **Shiqi Xiong (CHN)** – **6.49 m**  
10. **Mengyi Tan (CHN)** – **6.40 m**  

---

### Analysis & Reasoning  

**1. Alexis Brown** – The 2025 NCAA indoor champion has carried her momentum into the 2026 outdoor season. Her dominant victory at the Tom Jones Memorial on 17 April 2026 (7.07 m with a legal +1.4 m/s wind) is the best outdoor mark among all competitors this spring. Brown’s consistent 6.90+ indoor/outdoor jumps in 2025 (including a 6.91 at NCAA indoors and a 7.03 at Big 12) show she is peaking at the right time. Her speed (11.08 in the 100 m in 2025) also translates to elite runway velocity. She is the clear favourite to win in Shanghai.

**2. Natalia Linares** – The Colombian prodigy is on an upward trajectory after winning bronze at the 2025 World Championships (6.92 m) and bronze at the 2026 World Indoor Championships (6.80 m). She also jumped 6.95 m (legal, -0.1 wind) at the Bolivarian Games in December 2025. Her ability to produce big jumps under pressure and her youth (22 years old) suggest she will push Brown. Linares’s consistency in the 6.80–6.95 range makes her a near-lock for the podium.

**3. Monae' Nichols** – Nichols showed excellent early-season form with a 6.95 m legal jump and a 7.07 m wind-aided effort at the Miramar Invitational on 4 April 2026. While the 7.07 m is aided, the 6.95 m (legal, +0.3 wind) is her best legal mark since the 2025 US indoor season. She also won the 2025 US indoor title and jumped 6.88 m (legal) in June 2025. Her inconsistency (e.g., 6.33 m at Prefontaine in 2025) is a slight concern, but her recent indoor/outdoor trend is positive. She should challenge for a top-three spot.

**4. Larissa Iapichino** – The European indoor champion (2025) and World indoor silver medallist (2026) has been steady indoors (6.87 m at World Indoors in March) but has not yet jumped outdoors in 2026. Her 2025 outdoor peak was 7.06 m in Sicily, but she struggled in major finals (7th at 2025 Worlds with 6.56 m). Iapichino’s technique is polished, but she often underperforms on the Diamond League circuit relative to her potential. Expect a solid but not spectacular 6.83 m here.

**5. Claire Bryant** – The 2025 World indoor champion (6.96 m) had a brilliant 2025 outdoor season (7.03 m wind-aided, 6.91 m legal in Warsaw, 2nd at US Championships). However, her 2026 indoor season was more modest (best of 6.77 m, 3rd at US Indoors), and her only outdoor outing this spring was a 6.66 m at Tom Jones Memorial (17 April). She appears to be building form but is not yet at her 2025 level. A 6.80 m leap is realistic, placing her just off the podium.

**6. Quanesha Burks** – The 30-year-old veteran has no recorded outdoor performances in 2026 yet, but she finished 3rd at the 2025 US Championships (6.90 m) and placed 8th at the 2025 World Championships (6.60 m). Her best legal mark in 2025 was 6.90 m, but she also had several 6.60–6.70 m jumps. Without recent data, she is likely in the 6.70s range – a solid but not top-three level.

**7. Khaddi Sagnia** – The Swedish veteran (31) jumped 6.78 m indoors at the 2026 World Indoor Championships (4th place), her best mark since 2022. Outdoors in 2025, she struggled to break 6.70 m (best 6.69 m). Her consistency is decent (6.60–6.70 range), but she lacks the explosiveness to challenge for the win. Expect a mid-6.60s jump.

**8. Pauline Hondema** – The Dutch record-holder (6.91 m in July 2025) has failed to replicate that breakthrough since. Her 2026 indoor season was unremarkable (best 6.63 m at Dutch Indoors), and her 2025 outdoor average was ~6.50–6.70 m. She is capable of a big jump on her day, but her inconsistency (7th at 2025 Worlds with 6.60 m) suggests a mid-6.60s result here.

### Reasoning & Analysis

The field is exceptionally deep, with six athletes having thrown over 70 m in the past month. The key data point is the **Oklahoma Throws Series World Invitational (11 April 2026)** , which featured the majority of the contenders head-to-head. That meet provides the clearest comparative form line.

**Matthew Denny** (29) arrives as the hottest thrower on the circuit. He won the Oklahoma World Invitational with **73.58 m**, following a **74.04 m** two days earlier. His 2025 season included a **74.78 m** win in Ramona and a bronze‑medal finish at the 2024 Olympics. **Steven Richter** (22) is the revelation of 2026. The German U23 champion threw **74.00 m** (just 4 cm short of Denny) on 9 April and **72.47 m** in the World Invitational. He is the only athlete to match Denny’s peak in 2026. Richter also won the European Throwing Cup in March (67.29 m) and claimed the European U23 title in 2025. His youth and rapid progression suggest he will push Denny all the way, but Denny’s slight edge in consistency and big‑meet experience gives him the nod.

He tends to throw well in Shanghai (3rd in Doha 2025 with 66.92 m), but against this elite field a 72‑plus effort should secure third.

#### Strong Challengers with 71‑Meter Potential

**Lawrence Okoye** (34) has found a late‑career resurgence. His **71.88 m** in Oklahoma was his best since 2022, and he has been a consistent 66–67 m thrower on the European circuit. He should edge out Mattis on recent head‑to‑head form.

**Sam Mattis** (31) produced a startling **72.45 m** on 9 April – far above his official PB of 68.69 m. While that may be aided by conditions or the altitude in Ramona, his other 2026 marks (67.87 m, 69.75 m) are more typical. He likely settles for a high 60s to low 70s throw.

**Daniel Ståhl** (33) is a three‑time world champion and Olympic gold medalist. However, his single 2026 outing so far (64.20 m on 3 May) is alarming. Expect a throw around 69.80 m, which would be respectable but not enough to challenge the top.

The Xiamen 200 m brings together a mix of proven champions, emerging stars, and athletes seeking redemption. Her ability to go 22.17 in Chorzów (August 2025) and 22.07 in Shaoxing suggests she is peaking perfectly for this early-season Diamond League swing. The only minor concern is her fourth-place finish in the 100 m at the 2025 World Championships (10.88), but her 200 m consistency—winning her semi-final in 21.99 and taking bronze in the final (22.18)—proves she can deliver when it matters. Expect Jackson to control the race from the gun and close hard.

**Anavia Battle** has been the most consistent 200 m performer outside of Jackson over the past 12 months. She won the 200 m at the 2025 Xiamen Diamond League (22.41), the Shaoxing Diamond League (22.38), the Golden Gala (22.53), and the Meeting de Paris (22.27). More impressively, she placed 2nd at the 2025 US Championships (22.13) and 4th at the World Championships final (22.22) – meaning she finished higher than any other American in this race at those two major meets. Her 22.40 in Shaoxing (16 May 2026) was her third consecutive Diamond League race under 22.45. Battle’s ability to produce fast times in back-to-back meets, her strong curve, and her tactical maturity make her the clear second favourite. She will likely push Jackson through the first 100 m and hold off the chasing pack.

At just 23, she already owns a World Championships silver medal in the 200 m (22.14 in Tokyo 2025) and a 60 m indoor best of 7.04 (Toruń, Feb 2026) that signals exceptional speed endurance. Her semi-final at the 2025 World Championships (22.08) was faster than any woman in this field except Jackson’s 21.99. Her 22.48 in Shaoxing (16 May) was a slight step back, but that race came after a heavy indoor season and a transatlantic flight. With a week to adjust, Hunt’s turn of foot and improving strength should see her edge out the more experienced Richardson and Miller-Uibo for the bronze.

Her 22.42 in Shaoxing was her fastest outdoor 200 m since the 2023 season and a clear step in the right direction after a 2025 campaign where she struggled to break 22.5 (22.56 at US Trials, 22.42 in Shaoxing). However, she has not won a 200 m Diamond League race since 2023, and her performances against this specific field have been uneven: she was 4th in Shaoxing, 6th in the 100 m at the 2025 Silesia meet, and failed to make the 200 m final at the 2025 World Championships. Richardson’s explosive start is a weapon, but her ability to hold form over the final 50 metres against athletes like Battle and Hunt remains a question mark. She should be in the mix for 4th, but a podium finish would require a season-best performance.

Her 2026 outdoor opener was strong: 22.44 at the Florida Relays and 22.26 in Shaoxing (2nd place). That Shaoxing time was her fastest 200 m since 2022 and suggests she is rounding into form. However, Miller-Uibo’s resume is built on the 400 m, and her 200 m tactics often involve a patient first half followed by a furious finish – a strategy that works well against less experienced runners but can leave her vulnerable to faster starters like Jackson and Battle. Her 2025 season was interrupted by injury (she DNS'd the NACAC 400 m final), and she spent much of the year running 100 m and 200 m in lower-level meets (11.68 in Poland). Prandini’s consistency and experience are assets, but she no longer possesses the raw speed to challenge the top four. She will likely run a steady race, slot into 6th, and be content with a solid Diamond League points haul.

**Yujie Chen** is just 17 years old but already the Asian 100 m champion and Chinese national champion. Her 200 m best of 22.84 (Shaoxing, 16 May) is a remarkable time for her age, but she is still learning to compete against world-class fields. She ran 23.02 to win the National Games in November 2025, and her 22.84 in Shaoxing was a clear personal best. However, the intensity of the Diamond League environment and the caliber of her rivals – many of whom are full-time professionals with years of experience in high-pressure finals – will be a significant challenge. She should improve on her 2025 Xiamen run (22.99) but will likely fade in the final 50 m against more powerful athletes.

**Mckenzie Long** had a breakthrough 2025 season, winning the Ed Murphey Classic (21.93 legal) and making the World Championships semi-finals. However, her 2026 campaign has been disastrous: she finished 8th in Shaoxing (22.85) and 3rd at the USA Indoor Championships (60 m, 7.20). Her 22.85 in Shaoxing was nearly a full second slower than her personal best, and she has not broken 22.4 outdoors in 2026. The inconsistency that plagued her at the World Championships (8th in the final) seems to have carried over. She has the raw talent to run 22.0, but her recent form suggests she will struggle to match the likes of Hunt, Battle, and even Prandini.

**Torrie Lewis** is the youngest athlete in the field (20) and the reigning Australian 100/200 m champion. However, her 2026 season has been a struggle: she finished 9th in Shaoxing (23.25) and has not broken 22.8 outdoors this year. Her 2025 World Championships showed promise (22.56 in the heats), but she was well off the pace in the semi-finals (22.69). The Australian has good speed endurance (7.14 indoor 60 m) but seems to be struggling to translate that to outdoor 200 m success against elite competition. She will likely trail the field but gain invaluable experience.

**Conclusion:** Jackson’s class and recent form make her a near-certain winner. Battle’s consistency and proven Diamond League pedigree earn her silver. Hunt’s upward trajectory and world-class 200 m semi-final time give her the edge over the fading Miller-Uibo and the erratic Richardson. The rest of the field will be fighting for minor placings.

#### 1. Valarie Sion – The Undisputed Favorite  
Sion enters Rabat as the reigning Olympic and World champion, with a career defined by consistency at the highest level. Her 2025 season featured six Diamond League wins and a World gold (69.48 m). In 2026, she has already thrown 73.10 m (Oklahoma Throws Series, April) and 68.45 m to win the Xiamen Diamond League on 23 May – just one week before Rabat. That recent 68.45 m is a clear statement of form, and her ability to produce 68–70 m in competition is unmatched. Even a rare 6th-place finish (65.18 m) in early April was an anomaly; she rebounded immediately with 73.10 m. Sion’s North American record (73.52 m) and her head-to-head dominance over every rival in this field – she beat van Klinken at the 2025 World Championships (69.48 vs. 67.50) and has never lost to Tausaga or Ulrich in a Diamond League – make her a lock for the win. Expect a composed series around 68.75 m, possibly higher if conditions are favorable.

#### 2. Jorinde van Klinken – High Ceiling, Recent Dip  
Van Klinken owns the Dutch record (70.99 m, set in April 2026 at Oklahoma) and is the only athlete other than Sion to have cleared 70 m this season. However, her Xiamen performance (64.27 m, 3rd) was a significant drop, suggesting she may still be adjusting between shot put and discus. Despite that, her 2025 season was remarkably solid: she placed 2nd at Worlds (67.50 m) and was runner-up in multiple Diamond League meets (Paris, Zürich). Her 70.99 m shows she can peak, and Rabat likely offers a better environment than the long travel to China. Van Klinken tends to bounce back after a poor outing – after a 4th at Xiamen in 2025 (64.79 m), she threw 66.22 m the following week. Here, she should return to the 67 m range, finishing clear of the chasing pack.

#### 3. Laulauga Tausaga – Former Champion Seeking Consistency  
Tausaga is a 2023 World champion with a 2025 personal best of 70.72 m (2nd at Oklahoma), but her 2026 season has been erratic. After a promising 62.87 m in early May, she managed only 61.51 m at Xiamen (8th), her worst Diamond League result in years. This inconsistency – she also finished 6th at the 2025 World Championships (65.49 m) – stems from technical issues under pressure. Yet her peak is undeniable; she threw 70.72 m in a head-to-head with Sion’s 73.52 m in 2025. In Rabat, away from the long-haul travel that may have affected Xiamen, and with a week to refocus, Tausaga should improve to the mid-66 m range. She has historically outperformed Ulrich and Craft when dialed in, as shown by her 64.94 m at the 2025 Prefontaine Classic, where she beat both.

At 23, Ulrich is the youngest of the top Americans and has shown clear progression. Ulrich’s NCAA title in 2025 (65.82 m) and her 2nd-place finish at the 2024 Olympic Trials prove she rises to the occasion. Craft, 32, is a three-time European bronze medalist and a model of consistency. Her 2026 best is 66.03 m (Magdeburg, May 14), and she followed with 65.21 m the next weekend. At Xiamen she slipped to 63.96 m (6th), but that was her first outing of the year outside Europe. Craft’s 2025 season included a 68.10 m win in Wiesbaden and a 65.21 m at Worlds (8th). She rarely throws below 64 m and is reliable in big meets. Her style – smooth, rhythmic – suits the Rabat venue. Expect a rebound to the mid-65 m range, placing her ahead of the more volatile Jackson and Feng.

#### 6. Cierra Jackson – Talented but Inconsistent  
Jackson stunned the field with a 67.82 m at the 2025 Prefontaine Classic (2nd) and won the NCAA title (65.82 m). In 2026, she threw 67.25 m at Oklahoma (4th) but managed only 62.66 m at Xiamen (7th). However, her ceiling is high, and in a multi‑round competition she can produce a big throw. If she channels her Prefontaine form, she could challenge Craft. Given her recent 62–63 m trend, a 65.60 m is realistic – enough for 6th, but vulnerable to a poor round.

#### 7. Bin Feng – The Steady Chinese Thrower  
Feng, 31, was Olympic silver medalist in 2024 and World champion in 2022. She is less flashy than the Americans but extremely reliable in the 64–65 m range. At Xiamen on 23 May, she threw 65.03 m for 2nd place, her best of 2026. That performance came after a 63.28 m in May, showing upward trend. Her 2025 season included a 65.52 m at Worlds (7th) and consistent 64+ m in DL meets. Feng thrives in Asian conditions, but Rabat may be a step up in competition. She typically struggles against the depth of the US and European throwers – she was 5th at Xiamen 2025 (64.17 m) and 6th at Golden Gala (64.19 m). She should maintain her 65 m level but lacks the extra gear to overtake Jackson or Craft when they hit their marks.

#### 8. Marike Steinacker – Solid but Declining Form  
Steinacker, 33, placed 4th at the 2024 Olympics and is a perennial German champion. Her 2026 season opened with a 66.55 m (Oklahoma, April) and a 65.54 m in Magdeburg (May 14). However, her most recent results show a slight drop: 64.20 m in Wiesbaden (May 22) and 62.63 m in Rehlingen (May 24). That trend, plus a neutral‑warm‑up meet in Europe a week before Rabat, suggests she may be slightly fatigued. At Xiamen she did not compete, so she is fresh, but her peak is likely 65 m. She has been consistently behind Craft this season (Craft beat her in Magdeburg and Halle). Expect 65.05 m, just behind Feng.

#### 9. Erika Beistle – Impressive but Untested at This Level  
Beistle, 22, is a NCAA Division II standout who has rapidly improved. Her 2026 best is 66.72 m (May 10), and she threw 64.07 m at Xiamen (4th) – a remarkable result for someone with limited DL experience. That Xiamen mark was her first international Diamond League, and she handled it well. However, her consistency is questionable: she followed the 66.72 m with a 64.07 m, and earlier in the season she had a 64.54 m at Oklahoma. In a field with several proven 65+ m throwers, she may struggle to repeat that level under the pressure of a stronger lineup. Rabat will be her second DL, and the step up in opposition could lead to a slightly lower mark around 64.60 m, placing her 9th.

Kamga, 27, set her personal best (66.61 m) in the 2025 World final (4th). This season, she has been hovering around 64 m: 64.02 m at Xiamen (5th), 64.00 m in Varberg, and 64.22 m in 2025. She is a solid competitor but lacks the explosive marks of those above her. Her 2026 European Throwing Cup result (58.82 m) was poor, but she rebounded in Xiamen. She tends to produce mid‑64 m throws in non‑peak meets, and with no recent 65+ m, she falls behind the 65‑m group. Rabat will likely see her at 64.20 m, a typical result for her.

#### 11. Liliana Cá – Age and Form Decline  
Cá, 39, is past her prime. Her 2026 best is 61.89 m (European Champions Cup, May 23), and she has not thrown 65 m since 2023. Her 2025 season included a 65.35 m in Lisbon, but she was only 9th at Worlds (59.79 m). She has been a consistent 62–63 m thrower this spring, but that level is 2–3 meters behind the rest of the field. In a Diamond League with strong depth, she will struggle to break 63 m. Her experience may help in execution, but the physical decline is evident. 62.80 m is a fair estimate for 11th.

### Summary  
Sion’s dominance is unquestioned, while van Klinken and Tausaga possess the highest peaks. Ulrich and Craft offer reliable 65‑m consistency, and Jackson, Feng, and Steinacker fill the next tier. Beistle and Kamga are capable but not yet at the same level, and Cá rounds out the field. The Rabat meeting, typically held in warm conditions with a fast ring, should reward athletes who can maintain technique under pressure – an area where Sion, van Klinken, and Craft excel.

### Preview & Reasoning

She jumped 1.91 m in Xiamen (6th) and 1.84 m at Penn Relays. She has yet to prove she can transfer her indoor success to the outdoor circuit, where the wind and approach conditions change. She is a solid 1.90 m jumper, but in this field, that will slot her near the back. Her ceiling is 1.94 m, but she has not shown it outdoors recently.

Onnen, now 31, is a seasoned veteran but has never broken through to the elite echelon. Her personal best is 1.94 m outdoors, and she has jumped only 1.91 m in 2026 (indoor German title). She was 8th at World Indoors (1.89 m) and 9th in Xiamen (1.88 m). The field is simply too strong for her to compete for top-five finishes. She will likely start at 1.85 m and fail at 1.91 m, settling for 1.88 m. A respectable effort for an athlete past her prime.

- **Indoor-to-outdoor translation**: Hufnagel, Lake, and Cunningham have stronger indoor profiles than outdoor, while Mahuchikh, Levchenko, and Topić are equally good in both.

Rabat’s meet is early in the outdoor season, so athletes will not yet be at their absolute PBs. Expect solid, clean jumps rather than record attempts. Mahuchikh will control the bar, Levchenko will push her, and Topić will announce herself as a genuine contender for the Diamond League title.

The 2026 Rabat Diamond League 400m brings together a deep field featuring the reigning Olympic champion, a world‑record holder in the European record‑book, and a young Zambian who has been the most in‑form man on the circuit this spring. Based on recent head‑to‑head results, seasonal trajectories and each athlete’s performance trends, the predicted order leans heavily on the Xiamen Diamond League meeting just eight days earlier (23 May 2026).

**Muzala Samukonga** arrives in Rabat as the clear favourite. His 44.04 in Xiamen – a season’s best and just 0.07 off his 2025 best – was the fastest time any man in this field has run this year. That race also saw him defeat Zakithi Nene by 0.36 seconds and Bayapo Ndori by 0.84, establishing a clear hierarchy. Samukonga, still only 23 and already a Commonwealth and Olympic bronze medallist, has improved his consistency this spring: he ran 44.55 in Nairobi, 44.83 in Tokyo and then that 44.04. His closing speed, honed by frequent 200m races (including a 20.23 this season), makes him particularly dangerous over the final 100m. A slight further sharpening for Rabat puts him in the 44.01 range.

He has never been faster than Samukonga in any 2026 meeting, but his 44.40 in Xiamen was a respectable response after being beaten by Muzala. Nene’s 44.22 at the 2025 South African Championships and his 43.76 win in Nairobi last year show he has a higher gear, but he has not quite hit that level in 2026. Still, he is the second most consistent man in the field and should improve slightly in Rabat, perhaps to 44.25, especially with the motivation of a home‑continent crowd (though Rabat is North Africa, he’s a South African star). His 300m rust‑buster in Pretoria (31.85) hinted at good speed endurance.

He also has a strong tactical brain – witness his 43.98 at Grand Slam Track Miami last year. I expect him to run closer to 44.34, slotting behind Nene but ahead of the older stars.

SAC and **52.02** at LSU – both well inside her previous best. Her 300m hurdles win (37.40) on 8 May further confirms her sharpness over barriers. Cockrell’s 2025 campaign featured a 52.89 at US Champs and a 53.13 for 4th at Worlds; with improved raw speed, she should dip under 53.1 in Rabat.

**Savannah Sutherland**, only 22, is the wildcard. The Canadian record holder (50.62 flat 400m in 2025) and reigning NCAA champion (52.46) has immense talent. However, her 2025 World Championships were a disappointment (55.68 in the heats, DNQ). Since then she has focused on relays and has not raced a 400m hurdles in 2026. If she has refined her technique, her flat speed alone could challenge Cockrell. The prediction gives her a slight edge over Zapletalová based on her superior 400m flat credentials, but she remains unproven on the circuit this year.

**Emma Zapletalová** is the in‑form European. The 25‑year‑old Slovak owns a World bronze from Tokyo 2025 (53.00) and has been outstanding indoors this winter, clocking **50.78** (indoor 400m) and winning several World Indoor Tour meets. Her outdoor season began late, but she has the consistency and race‑craft to run in the low‑53s. She beat Cockrell at Worlds, but Cockrell’s improved flat speed flips that head‑to‑head in Rabat.

**Gianna Woodruff** (32) is the wily veteran. The Pan American champion ran a stunning **52.66** in the World semi‑final last year and backed it up with 53.34 in the final. Her 2026 flat 400m times (52.43 at LSU, 52.46 at Mt. SAC) show she is in similar shape. Woodruff’s ability to rise to occasion in championship‑style races makes her a threat, though she sometimes struggles in highly tactical Diamond League finals. Expect a solid 53.4.

**Rushell Clayton** (33) is a two‑time World bronze medalist with a PB of 52.81. She looked sharp in April with a 51.85 flat 400m at Tom Jones, but her 2025 hurdles times (best 53.81 at Jamaican Champs) were a step below her peak. At this age, she may lack the final‑gear speed to challenge the younger trio ahead. Still, her experience ensures a competitive mark around 53.6.

**Andrenette Knight** (29) has been consistent but not spectacular. Her 2025 best of 53.67 (Rome) and 2026 flat 400m of 52.04 (Gibson McCook) suggest a 53.8‑54.0 finish. She is a reliable second‑tier contender but has not shown the breakthrough needed to crack 53.3.

**Amalie Iuel** (31) opened her 2026 hurdles season with a solid **54.12** in Nairobi (24 April). Her World semi‑final of 54.28 last year was strong, and she ran 53.26 indoor over 400m. She is consistent but lacks the top‑end speed of the leaders; 54.1 is a fair projection.

**Ayomide Folorunso** (29) ran 51.98 indoors this winter and had a 54.21 at the 2025 Golden Gala, but her outdoor hurdles have often hovered around 54.3‑54.7. She may struggle to match the pace of the top six.

**Naomi van den Broeck** (29) had a quiet start to 2026, with no outdoor hurdles results yet. Her 2025 best of 53.70 (Worlds final) is respectable, but she has not shown recent form to suggest a breakthrough. A time in the mid‑54s seems likely.

**Key Head‑to‑Head Comparisons**  
- At the 2025 World final: Zapletalová (53.00) > Cockrell (53.13) > Woodruff (53.34) > van den Broeck (53.70).  
- 2026 flat 400m: Cockrell (51.49) > Sutherland (50.62 in 2025) > Clayton (51.85) > Woodruff (52.43) > Knight (52.04) – but hurdles translation favours Cockrell and Woodruff.  
- Recent hurdles form: Woodruff (52.66 semi 2025) > Cockrell (52.89 US Champs) > Zapletalová (53.00) > Knight (53.67).  

Cockrell’s dramatic flat‑speed improvement and strong hurdle rhythm from her 300m hurdles win gives her the edge. Sutherland’s raw talent could push her close, but lack of 2026 hurdles racing makes her a slight risk. Zapletalová and Woodruff will battle for bronze, with the Slovak’s indoor momentum tipping the scale. Clayton and Knight round out the top six, while Iuel, Folorunso, and van den Broeck complete the field in a tightly bunched pack. The Rabat track should deliver fast times, and the top three could all dip under 53.3.

Jackson arrives in Rabat on a stunning run of form. Her back-to-back Diamond League victories in Shaoxing (22.07) and Xiamen (21.87) – the latter just a week ago – show she is at her sharpest. As the second-fastest woman in history over 200m (21.41) and the reigning world champion in the event, she has both the pedigree and the current momentum. Her 100m win in Rabat a year earlier (11.04) also demonstrates comfort on this track. At 31, she still dominates the bend and finishes with signature power. Expect another controlled performance in the 21.9–22.0 range.

After a solid 22.44 in April, she improved to 22.26 in Shaoxing and then 22.04 in Xiamen – both times finishing directly behind Jackson. That 22.04 is her fastest 200m since 2021 and shows she is rediscovering her top-end speed. Her immense strength from the 400m gives her a powerful final 100m, but she still lacks Jackson’s pure top gear on the turn. She will push hard but likely settle for second again in ~22.09.

**Third: Cambrea Sturgis**  
Sturgis has been the most impressive American in the 200m this season, running 22.09 (+1.7) at the Baylor Invitational and 21.93 (+1.7) in Nairobi – both within legal wind limits. Additionally, her 21.93 came at altitude (Nairobi ~1,660m), which can flatter times slightly. Still, she is clearly in sub-22.2 shape and should outpace the rest of the field.

Long’s 2025 season included a wind-legal 21.93 (+1.2) at the Ed Murphey Classic and a 22.12 in the US Championships heats, but she has struggled in 2026. Her last two DL outings – 22.85 in Shaoxing and 22.63 in Xiamen – reflect inconsistency and perhaps a lack of peak fitness. At 25, she has the raw talent to challenge the top three, but her recent form does not inspire confidence. She will likely finish mid-22.7, ahead of the next group.

White’s best 200m this season is 22.61 (-2.0) from Tom Jones, and she ran 22.68 in Gaborone. She is a reliable sprinter who placed 2nd in the 100m at US Championships in 2025, but her 200m has never been her strongest event (7th at USAs in 2025). She lacks the explosive turn speed of the top three and tends to fade in the final 60m. Expect a time around 22.83.

**Sixth: Audrey Leduc**  
The Canadian record-holder (22.36) has not raced a 200m outdoors this season, focusing on 100m and relays. Her most recent 200m was an indoor 23.25 in February, and she ran 10.93w in the 100m in April. Without a recent 200m outing, she will struggle to match her PB. Her last Diamond League 200m was in 2024, and she has not shown the sharpness needed to break 22.8 here. A 22.94 is plausible.

**Seventh: Torrie Lewis**  
The 20-year-old Australian has had a tough start to the 2026 Diamond League circuit, finishing 9th in Shaoxing (23.25) and 9th in Xiamen (23.25). She set a 100m national record (11.08) in 2025 and has potential, but her 200m form has plateaued. She lacks the strength and experience of the older athletes and will likely bring up the rear in ~23.28.

### Race Preview & Analysis

#### The Contenders: Tier 1 – The Clear Favourite

**Emmanuel Wanyonyi**  
There is no plausible argument against Wanyonyi as the winner. At 21, he is the reigning Olympic and World champion, already tied for second on the all‑time list (1:41.11). His 2025 campaign was staggering: he won six Diamond League 800m races, including a blistering **1:41.44 in Monaco** and a **1:41.86 World final** in Tokyo. He showed versatility by winning a cross‑country race (6:14 for 2km) and running **3:34.11 over 1500m** in Nairobi just five weeks before this Rabat race. That 1500m time indicates he is in superb aerobic shape. Wanyonyi has also proven he can win in Rabat specifically – he was 3rd here in 2025 (1:43.37), a relatively “slow” run for him, but that was early in his season. Now, with a full year of maturity and a peak‑level 1500m under his belt, he will be sharper. Expect him to sit just off the pace, then unleash his trademark 26‑second final 200m to win comfortably in the low‑1:42 range.

#### Tier 2 – The Podium Challengers

**Max Burgin**  
The 23‑year‑old Brit has quietly built a résumé that places him as Wanyonyi’s most credible threat. His **1:42.36 in London (2025)** – where he finished 3rd behind Wanyonyi and Marco Arop – is a genuine world‑class mark. He also ran 1:42.42 to place 2nd in Zurich and 1:42.29 in the World final (6th place, but the depth was immense). Crucially, Burgin ran **1:43.34 in Rabat in 2025** – faster than Wanyonyi’s 1:43.37 that day. He knows the track. His 2026 form is less documented, but he is young and trending upward. If he can stay close to Wanyonyi through 600m, he has the finishing speed to hold off the rest. I expect him to be the only one within a second of Wanyonyi.

**Donavan Brazier**  
The 28‑year‑old former world champion (2019) is a fascinating case. His 2025 was a comeback year: he won the US title in **1:42.16** – his fastest since his AR days – and placed 3rd in the World semis. However, his 2026 has been inconsistent. He ran 1:45.03 in Los Angeles in late May 2026, which is well below his best. The Brighton track season suggests he might not yet be in peak Diamond League shape. But Brazier has proved he can rise to the occasion; his 1:42.16 is the second‑fastest time in the field after Wanyonyi’s PBs. If he finds his rhythm, he can dip under 1:42.5. I’m placing him 3rd because his ceiling is higher than anyone else in this tier, but his recent form is a slight concern.

#### Tier 3 – The Sub‑1:43 Group

**Gabriel Tual**  
The French European Champion has a PB of **1:41.61** (2024) – faster than anyone here except Wanyonyi. But his 2025 season tells a different story: he placed 4th in Oslo (1:43.09), 4th in Stockholm (1:42.72), and then faded to 10th in Monaco (1:44.17) and 11th in Budapest (1:45.10). In the World final, he was only 7th (1:43.47). His 2026 indoor season was modest (48.64 in 400m, no standout 800m). Tual is a brilliant racer when confident, but he seems to be struggling to replicate his 2024 form. He will be in the mix for 4th, but he lacks the consistency to challenge the top three.

**Kethobogile Haingura**  
The Botswana runner is one of the most consistent performers in the field. In 2025, he ran **1:43.75 in Miami**, 1:43.82 in Rabat, 1:43.58 in Oslo, and 1:43.61 in Stockholm – all within a tenth of each other. He also placed 2nd in the Shaoxing Diamond League in May 2026 (1:43.89). He is reliable, has good tactical sense, and rarely runs a bad race. His ceiling might be 1:42.8, but he lacks the explosive kick of Wanyonyi or Burgin. Expect him to be in the top five, battling Tual for 4th.

**Eliott Crestan**  
The Belgian indoor silver medalist (2025 World Indoors) has superb speed and confidence. His outdoor 2025 was excellent: he won in Madrid (1:43.79), Brussels (1:43.91), and ran 1:43.83 indoors in 2026. However, his outdoor best is only **1:42.43** (2024 NR). In major finals, he has a tendency to fade – he was 8th in the World semis in 2025 (1:44.56). He is a strong racer but not yet a consistent sub‑1:43 performer. He’ll fight for 5th/6th.

#### Tier 4 – The Experienced Veterans and Rising Talent

**Mark English**  
The 32‑year‑old Irish record holder is a wily veteran. He ran **1:43.85 in Shaoxing** (May 2026, 2nd place) and 1:43.92 in Hengelo (2025). He has good endurance and rarely panics. However, his top speed is limited compared to the younger guns: his 2025 best was 1:43.37 (Gyulai Memorial). He will be competitive but lacks the kick to break into the top five.

**Slimane Moula**  
The Algerian former African champion has a PB of 1:43.38, but that was set in 2023. Since then, his results have been middling: 1:42.77 in Stockholm (2025) is his best in two years, but he placed 8th in the World semis and only 5th indoors in 2026. He seems to have plateaued. He can run 1:43.5, but cannot go lower.

**Yanis Meziane**  
The 23‑year‑old Frenchman is rising. He ran **1:43.71 in Budapest (2025)** and 1:43.82 in Madrid. He was 6th in the World semis. He is still improving, but he lacks the heavyweight experience of the top group. He will press early and might fade slightly, settling for 9th.

**Francesco Pernici**  
The Italian U23 standout ran 1:44.05 in Brussels (2025) and 1:44.39 in Madrid. He is promising but has yet to break 1:44.0. His 2026 season is just beginning – he ran 1:46.77 in Udine. He is not ready for this level yet.

**Abdelati el Guesse & Patryk Sieradzki**  
Both have PBs around 1:44.8, but their recent form is poor. El Guesse has a best of 1:44.19 in 2025 but was 8th in his World heat. Sieradzki’s 2025 was plagued by DNFs – he failed to finish in Monaco, London, Zürich, and multiple other meets. His 2026 outdoor best is only 1:46.69. They will be well back.

**Imad Bouchajda**  
The 18‑year‑old Moroccan is a tremendous talent – he won silver at the African Championships (1:45.62) in May 2026. But he is a junior stepping into a Diamond League elites. He will likely run a PB (1:45.85 predicted) but cannot contend.

---

### Key Tactical Scenario

Wanyonyi will likely push a steady pace, perhaps with a 49.5‑50.0 first lap. Burgin and Brazier will cover him. Tual, Haingura, and Crestan will form the chasing pack. The real test comes at the 600m mark: if Wanyonyi kicks with 200m to go, only Burgin has the speed to respond. Brazier, if mentally sharp, can close hard but may start too far back. The rest will be sprinting for position in the final straight, with gaps opening up.

**Final verdict:** Wanyonyi dominates as expected. Burgin holds off Brazier for 2nd. The rest follow in a tightly packed, mid‑1:43 to low‑1:44 battle, with Haingura’s consistency giving him the edge over the erratic Tual and Crestan.

## Race Preview & Reasoning

### The Favourites
**Soufiane el Bakkali** (MAR, 29) is the headline act on home soil. He dominated this very meeting in 2025 with an 8:00.70 victory – the fastest time of the season by any man in the field. While his 2026 form is untested in steeplechase, his pedigree as a two‑time Olympic champion and 2022/23 world champion cannot be ignored. He also won the 2025 Rabat race by a clear margin, and the home crowd will drive him again. The only blemish is his narrow defeat to Beamish in the Tokyo 2025 World final (8:33.95 vs 8:33.88), but that was a tactical, slow affair; el Bakkali is the superior racer when the pace is on, as evidenced by his 8:00.70. Expect him to push the pace early and hold off all challengers.

**Geordie Beamish** (NZL, 29) enters as the reigning 2025 World Champion. He beat el Bakkali head‑to‑head in Tokyo, which gives him a psychological edge. However, his season‑opening indoor campaign in 2026 was only modest (14th in the World Indoor 3000m, 7:45.05). He has shown he can win in a slow, tactical race, but the Rabat Diamond League historically rewards fast times. His 8:09.64 PB and lack of a sub‑8:05 steeplechase suggests he may lack the raw speed of el Bakkali over a true fast pace. He will likely sit behind the Moroccan and kick hard, but finishing second is realistic.

**Frederik Ruppert** (GER, 28) was second in the 2025 Rabat race in 8:01.49, just 0.79 seconds behind el Bakkali. He also ran a 10,000m of 27:24.53 in March 2026 – outstanding endurance that will help him maintain a strong rhythm late in the race. His 2025 World Championships final was disappointing (12th, 8:39.83), but he rebounded with a 8:01.49 in Rabat, showing that meet suits him. As the second‑fastest returner from last year’s Rabat, he should repeat his podium finish.

### The Kenyan Threat
**Edmund Serem** (KEN, 18) is the youngest in the field but already a World Championships bronze medallist (2025, 8:34.56). He ran 8:04.00 in Monaco 2025, the fastest time of any teenager in the world. However, his 2026 start has been unspectacular – only 8:25.85 in Nairobi – suggesting he may still be building form. He has enormous raw talent but faces tougher, more experienced rivals in a fast early‑season race. Fourth is a fair projection.

**Simon Kiprop Koech** (KEN, 22) is a two‑time Kenyan champion (2023, 2025) and ran 8:07.12 in Xiamen 2025. He also finished second at the 2026 Kip Keino Classic (8:15.71). He lacks the consistent sub‑8:08 performances of the top three, but his solid finishing speed should earn him fifth ahead of the fading Firewu.

### The Ethiopian & Moroccan Challengers
**Samuel Firewu** (ETH, 21) burst onto the scene with an 8:05.61 victory in Xiamen 2025, but his form has since declined. He failed to finish a 5000m in 2026, ran only 8:39.28 at the Ethiopian Championships, and managed just 8:41.67 at the African Championships (losing to Ben Yazide). A return to 8:05 form is unlikely; he will struggle to hold off Koech.

**Salah Eddine ben Yazide** (MAR, 22) is the African Championships silver medallist (8:41.02) and ran a strong 8:06.44 in Monaco 2025. He finished fifth at the 2025 World Championships – a high floor – but his 8:41 in Accra was a major step back. He will be motivated at home, but his recent marks suggest 8:10–8:11.

### The Veterans & European Contingent
**Mohamed Amin Jhinaoui** (TUN, 28) has a solid record in Diamond Leagues (8:08.27 in Monaco 2025) and recently ran 13:21 for 5000m – raw speed that could help in the final lap. He is consistent but lacks the top‑end brilliance of the leaders.

**Daniel Arce** (ESP, 33) is a seasoned campaigner, having run 8:10.58 in Rabat 2025. However, he DNF’d in the World Championships heats and failed to finish a 10,000m in May 2026. At 33, his best years are behind him, but he remains competitive for a top‑10 spot.

**Djilali Bedrani** (FRA, 32) has shown versatility (3:36.63 1500m) but his steeplechase form has dipped – 8:11.52 in Rabat 2025 and no sub‑8:10 since 2023. The veteran **Abraham Kibiwot** (KEN, 29) – Olympic bronze medallist in 2024 – has been inconsistent in 2025/26, with a DNF at the World final and only 8:30.86 in Nairobi. He may struggle to match his 8:05.51 PB.

**Matthew Wilkinson** (USA, 27) qualified for the 2024 Olympics and ran 8:10.23 in Monaco 2025. His 2026 indoor times (7:35.77 for 3000m) indicate good speed, but he is relatively inexperienced at this level and often fades in deep fields. **Nicolas-Marie Daru** (FRA, 37) is the veteran French champion; his 8:10.69 in 2025 shows he still has a competitive edge, but age and a heavy early‑season schedule (including cross country) may limit him to 8:16–8:17.

### The Bottom of the Field
**Baptiste Fourmont** (FRA, 26) and **Alexis Miellet** (FRA, 30) – the latter the 2024 European champion – have both run 8:12–8:13 in 2025 but have shown little 2026 steeplechase form (Miellet focusing on 1500m). **Mohamed Tindouft** (MAR, 32) has a history of DNFs and only an 8:21.01 best in 2025. **Faid el Mostafa** (MAR, 25) ran 8:14.04 in Stockholm 2025 but DNF’d in Monaco and his 2026 is unknown. **Abderrafia Bouassel** (MAR, 24) has DNF’d in every 2025 steeplechase start – he will likely finish well back, if at all.

### Race Dynamics
With el Bakkali, Ruppert, and Serem likely to push a brisk pace from the gun, the race will probably be run in 8:00–8:05 territory. Beamish will try to stay in contact and use his acceleration, but el Bakkali’s comfort on this track and his ability to control the race should give him the win. The fireworks will come in the final 400m, where el Bakkali’s superior water‑jump technique and home‑crowd lift will prove decisive.
